etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English prevailen, from Old French prevaler, from Latin praevaleō (“be very able or more able, be superior, prevail”), from prae (“before”) + valeō (“be able or powerful”). Displaced native Old English rīcsian.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be superior in strength, dominance, influence, or frequency; to have or gain the advantage over others; to have the upper hand; to outnumber others.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 17:11:
quote.text: And it came to pass, when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed; and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.

quote.citation: 2022 February 27, Phil McNulty, “Chelsea 0-0 Liverpool”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: Liverpool created a host of chances and had a Joel Matip goal ruled out for a foul and offside in an incident-packed game that went right down to the wire before Jurgen Klopp's side prevailed.

quote.citation: 2019 January 14, “Exploring the SCP Foundation: SCP-2935 - O, Death” (0:36 from the start), in The Exploring Series‎[2], archived from the original on 25 March 2023:
quote.text: There are a number of SCPs and tales that look at potential apocalypses, but rarely with such totality as SCP-2935, a parallel dimension in which death prevailed.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be current, widespread, or predominant; to have currency or prevalence.
(intransitive) To succeed in persuading or inducing.

quote.citation: 1749, Henry Fielding, The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling:
quote.text: Jones began to be very importunate with the lady to unmask; and at length having prevailed, there appeared not Mrs Fitzpatrick, but the Lady Bellaston herself.
